REPORT ON OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of a report published yesterday which seriously challenged the ability of last year's or this year's government youth programs to deal effectively with the basic problems of youth unemployment, in view of the discrimination with which the evaluation charged those programs, and in view of the high figure of unemployment among those under the age of 24, reaching 11 per cent last year, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Lundrigan), the following motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43:
1.	This House request the Secretary of State to table the Cohen Report on Summer '71 forthwith.
2.	Refer the evaluation of Summer '71 to a Standing Committee.
3.	The Secretary of State maintain his undertaking to call a broadly-based federal-provincial community conference on youth programming.
4.	Direct the Secretary of State to call a meeting of provincial ministers and members of the business community so that a meaningful program of long range youth employment initiatives might be put into force at the earliest possible date.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a question of urgent and pressing necessity. maintopic: POLICIES TO ACHIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT TARGET RECOMMENDED BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister accept the target and the definition of the Economic Council of Canada which describes full employment as being 3.8 per cent, and does the government intend to pursue policies which will achieve this level of employment by 1975 as recommended by the Economic Council of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: POLICIES TO ACHIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT TARGET RECOMMENDED BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, any level of unemployment is unfortunate for the percentage of people who are unemployed and therefore there is no reason why I would accept a target of 3.8 per cent. If we could go lower we would prefer it. In fact, just a couple of years ago there was less than 3.8 per cent unemployment in some parts of Canada and more in other parts. Therefore I cannot accept this target. What we want to do is, to achieve the lowest possible rate of unemployment consistent with stable growth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really very sorry to break up this interesting question period but the rules allow me no alternative. May I point out to the House, through you, Mr. Speaker, that it may well be that this subject matter is not as colourful and controversial as some members might like. Nevertheless, it is the view of the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition that every once in a while during the course of a parliament some effort should be made to come to the aid of the beleaguered taxpayer.
It seems to us that there are an awful lot of taxpayers. To paraphrase what Abraham Lincoln said, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) must love the taxpayers because he has made so many of them. In any event, this matter is surely of the essence in view of the fact there is no doubt at all that there are a great many responsible people who are concerned about the performance of the economy and that the real problems of unemployment, inflation and economic growth, not only in Canada but in the United States and Europe, are not responding to orthodox remedies.
There is a lack of confidence. There is lack of confidence on the part of the business community in this government. While the government may be temporarily altering its stance, we note that this is only temporary. There is lack of confidence on the part of consumers in this government. They lack the confidence that the government cqn take the essential steps to place under some control the accelerating cost of living. Finally, there is lack of confidence on the part of the taxpayer that this government has the capacity or the will to check the deadly twin viruses of increasing taxation and inefficient handling of the taxpayers' money. Attempts by the Parliament of Canada at restraint and scrutiny have become a mockery and a farce. There needs to be a new flowering of the strength of parliament to deal with this very serious problem.
Governments more and more seem to be bland, anonymous bureaucrats with the power to command the lives and take the property of people, to tell them what do do and how to do it, and there seems very little hope of getting any change. The end result is inevitable: there is cynicism, frustration, militancy and often confrontation and violence in the streets. People will therefore turn their faces away from government as we know it, from the legislative system and the whole democratic process, and many of them are.
But despite all the warts and defects of the parliamentary system, I suggest all the other methods by which

people contrive to order their affairs are infinitely worse. The neat trick is to take what we have and make it better, make it work, and, like the ideal of justice, make it be seen to be working. The infinite wisdom of the ages lies in all of the people in society, and the problem is to find and use these truths as the basis for the rules under which society operates. People need to know this. They need to know and to believe that the system can be delicately tuned and made responsive to their views; that not only the majority but the minority, even the individual, who has a cause to plead, a wrong to right and a proposal to urge, will be provided with some means by which to do so. This can be the parliamentary structure when it has the freedom and the mechanism to operate. But that is what is lacking today.
The parliamentary system of government should be like the two pans of a scale, evenly balanced between the executive branch on the one side, and the legislative branch on the other side. That is a principle that, I think, is acceptable to all people. But what has happened? There has been a grotesque distortion. There has been poured into the pan on the executive side of the scales more and more weight; on the other side, there has been a taking away from the legislative branch of many of the powers and authorities it requires. In the result, this distortion is very apparent in the limited way that this parliament can check expenditures and scrutinize the estimates of government. I know government needs to have power, strength and the ability to act quickly. But there needs to be, as the Prime Minister himself said, a countervailing force. This is what we lack and it is what this party proposes to do something about.
Recently the Prime Minister, in a speech made to the National Conference on the Law, said something which I regard with great concern. These are his words:
Perhaps in some instances the adversary system, so revered by lawyers, is a counter-productive element in the political process; for example, in relations between various levels of government.
Further on in his speech the Prime Minister confirmed that view. I question the validity of that assertion. The doctrine of infallibility comes, of course, easily to those who occupy the chairs of state. Such being the case, the only safety lies, in part, in the adversary system, with the ability to press for change, to refine, to restrict or in any way to cope with the bureaucratic despotism, stupidity, inaction, stealth and secrecy which from time to time characterize this administration. The white paper on taxation was changed largely because of the adversary system. When in turn that white paper was translated into a bill, there were important changes made in the bill as a result of pressure exerted by people both outside the House and inside this House. That is the virtue of the adversary system.
That is not all, Mr. Speaker. I could list a number of issues that have benefitted from this system, such as the government reorganization bill, Bill C-176, the grain stabilization bill, and, of course, the infamous bill that this government brought in over a year ago in an attempt to curtail the power and independence of the Auditor General. Because of the adversary system, and because of pressure outside the House and representations made in the House, the government was compelled to withdraw that
March 7, 1972

bill. Hearing statements of this kind made from the Prime Minister and supported by his colleagues, and noting many of the trends of the government in Ottawa today, it is time for all good men who believe in the parliamentary system to draw together and challenge the government.
Without in any way restricting the list, let me outline some of the more dangerous changes that we see taking place from day to day. There are the fundamental changes in the character of legislation, where today all too often bills are merely enabling acts, vague declarations of principle, with the dry bones being fleshed out by orders in council, decrees and regulations made by the bureaucracy in the secret places of their private offices without the knowledge, consent or advice of parliament. In that regard I urge the government to take steps at once to establish the scrutiny committee that is set up by the statutory instruments act. That committee will form one of the bulwarks against this kind of despotism which we so often encounter in this country.
We must also consider the growth, at an abnormal rate, of this bureaucracy. Their elite have now become the high priests of our society and we build great, shining temples to them throughout the land and worship before the altars in those temples. Then, we must consider, as well, the enlargement of the office and the growth in power of the leader of the government so that, through the bureaucratic machine at his command and by the skilful use of the media, he will always appear larger than life; also, the refusal of government to furnish people with proper and adequate information of the public affairs of the land. Further, we must consider the lack of adequate checks and restraints on public spending.
That old grey mare the Treasury Board has recently unbent enough to put out, during the last two sessions, a shiny new pamphlet called, "How Your Tax Dollar is Spent".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I now quote from a column recently written by that great Canadian columnist, Charles Lynch. He wrote this soon after the latest blue book of estimates was inflicted upon Parliament:
The unfortunate thing is, however, that while the costs of government continue to go up, there is no sign of an increase in government efficiency.
-the size of the public payroll today, relative to the amount of work being produced, is a bigger disgrace than ever. Glassco was too late, and nothing can save the taxpayer now, or ever.
Time is of the essence in debates of this kind, so that I will simply limit myself to outlining some of the areas where there is ground for legitimate complaint on behalf of the taxpayers of this country about the way their money is being spent by the government, and the way in which estimates for those expenditures are placed before Parliament and approved.
In this connection, as well, we shall need to consider the unholy mess disclosed by the secret memorandum from the Deputy Director of Information Canada; certain expenditures on behalf of the Department of National Defence relating particularly to the Bonaventure, the hydrofoil vessel and the DDH destroyer program, which is still pending; some of the projects contained in the local initiatives program; the manpower training and unemployment insurance benefits fiasco, and the housing program; and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and its method of making grants and providing subsidies. If I have an opportunity, and if time permits, I will go into details with respect to these matters later, Mr. Speaker. Some of my colleagues who will follow me will deal particularly with some of the areas I have mentioned, and will outline clearly sufficient evidence to convince even hon. members opposite that the government is stupid. They will establish beyond any reasonable doubt incompetence, mismanagement, waste, stupidity and gross carelessness in the payment of taxpayers' money.
It is the duty of an opposition to be critical, Mr. Speaker, to point out errors and defects in the operations of government. I submit that Her Majesty's loyal opposition has, during the course of this Parliament, gone beyond this and from time to time made a series of alternative proposals and suggestions which will be found incorporated in the various amendments which we have offered, either with respect to legislation or in the form of various opposition day motions we have moved. I am not suggesting that they contain the sum total of our alternative policies. I want to make the point, in answer to those who have indicated that we have not suggested any alternative remedies, that a full examination of the parliamentary records and of Hansard will make it abundantly clear that we have discharged our proper responsibilities and offered rational alternatives. Why, then, have some of these programs slipped through? Why are they being maladministered? Why is money being paid out as it is now being paid out? And, what can be done about it?
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, the committee system has not worked as was expected and many of its original proponents now doubt its value. I have talked to hon.

March 7, 1972
Control of Government Expenditures members opposite, who agree with me. Many of them, as I say, doubt its total value, particularly in so far as estimates are concerned. Mr. Speaker, there must be changes. All we have today is a minuet of committees. In many instances there is no opportunity and no means for hon. members to come to grips with the question of estimates, payments and expenditures. The basic principle governing supply, a principle that has come down to us through the ages, has been eliminated. This principle is that supply ought to be held up until basic grievances raised in this place by members of the House on behalf of the people of Canada have been answered. At present, Sir, there is no real opportunity for this to be done.
At present, estimates must be passed by a calendar date. Even if there has not been adequate study with regard to some of the items, and in many instances there certainly has not, all the votes are automatically deemed to have been passed by a certain date. In committees, the intention was to provide government members with an opportunity to be objective and independent, and avoid the party whip. This has not been the case. Government members fall neatly into file and toe the party line when estimates are challenged. A recent column written by George Bain in the Toronto Globe and Mail demonstrated this. He said in part:
-the principle of responsibility always looming, the committees in the end will report on any vital matter precisely on party lines.-
-But it would be worthwhile to examine, openly, to see whether it would be beyond Canadian ingenuity to devise a system which, by reducing to a very small handful the occasions on which a government might be defeated in the House and have to give up power, would permit some relaxation of the dead hand of party discipline as now applied.
I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will heed the message and relax the stern discipline under which all members are restrained when estimates are discussed, so that backbenchers on the government side in particular may be free to vote according to the dictates of their consciences rather than according to the way they are told to vote.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: You people had better watch your own discipline.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Let me talk for a moment about supplementary estimates. Today we were given supplementary estimates B, involving some $433 million. Supplementary Estimates A were tabled in the House on November 19, 1971 and totalled some $872 million. In other words, by virtue of these supplementary estimates, more that $1 billion has been added to the spending program of this government. What opportunity do hon. members have to deal with these supplementary estimates? What has happened, Mr. Speaker?
The estimates of 25 departments were contained in Supplementary Estimates A which totalled altogether $872 million odd. There were 87 votes in all in those supplementary estimates. Because of the limitation of time pursuant to our Standing Orders, only 32 of those votes were considered. We never discussed 55 of them. They were never debated, never questioned. Not a single question was put in the committee, largely because of the fixed date for passing the estimates which governed the work of the committee. The estimates were out of the committee

on December 7 and were the subject of an appropriation bill in this House on December 9. Mr. Speaker, that was shabby treatment. That was not good enough. The people of Canada are being ill served by Parliament when the rules established by this government permit sharp practices by the government and even encourage this to happen.
There is a great lack of detailed information in the estimates. I shall not go into the details of that, but I defy even members of this House, after looking at the estimates to comprehend what is involved. They are full of gobbledygook. Those people in the Treasury Board who know about them may understand them, but to the average member of the public and even to members of this House they simply do not make sense. I am not alone in saying this. The Auditor General said it in many of his reports to this House. The Public Accounts Committee has said it also on a great many occasions. I suggest that a very serious look should be taken at this particular problem, so that when we examine these estimates they will be comprehensible and we will have the capacity to deal with them.
In addition to that, I suggest that the estimates of at least four or five departments must be brought to the House each session by way of Committee of Supply. These should be at the choice of the opposition. This would mean that, during the course of the average Parliament of four years, more than half the departments of government would have had their estimates discussed in the wider forum of the House of Commons. I am not suggesting at this time that we revert entirely to the old system. We may consider this, at least as a half-way house, but I think it is absolutely essential that commencing this session at least four or five departments should have their estimates considered in the House in Committee of Supply. Then, there should be a vote on every motion brought in by the opposition parties on the 25 opposition days, although only six of these would be construed as being non-confidence motions. There is no reason the government should not be compelled to take a stand and that all members be counted. This could be done if it were clearly understood that these were not non-confidence motions. At the present time, unless there is a motion on which there is to be a vote, the procedure becomes more and more futile so far as the opposition is concerned.
I have already indicated that in my view the form of the estimates should be changed to conform with the proposals made by the Public Accounts Committee and by the Auditor General. In that regard there is one important suggestion I make to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). Members of this House, members of committees and the public should be aware of the present estimated cost of programs. We have often seen the situation where some large program is introduced with a blaring of trumpets and loud hallelujahs. It is rumoured that the cost will be X million dollars. Each year we find in the estimates a limited amount of money included to cover that particular year's work on that project. What we do not know, however, from year to year is by how much the cost of that project escalates and, by the time the project is completed, we learn to our dismay and certainly to the
March 7, 1972

dismay and anxiety of the taxpayer that it cost not X million of dollars but rather four times X million of dollars.
I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that in each vote of the estimates of this kind there should be included the original project cost, the present estimated cost and any proposals or thoughts which may be in the mind of the Treasury Board about the final cost. Such information should be available in clear and specific language to members of the House and the public so that they would have knowledge of the ultimate cost of the project. In this way, the taxpayers would know what they are facing, and then if they wished to object through us as their representatives we would be in a position to do so, basing the objection on facts.
There should be a moratorium on dollar items. In the supply items given to us today by the Treasury Board we find 12 dollar items.

I stand corrected. I have not had an opportunity to examine them. I noticed 12 at first blush. We all know what dollar items are. The government brings in an item for $1 and within the limited wording of a vote in the estimates there is a provision for spending which should be contained in legislation. I suggest there is no reason, save in cases of emergency, that the government should not with proper timing and proper understanding place legislation before the House. We have an example in Information Canada. We have an example in the local initiatives program. There are dozens of examples costing hundreds of millions of dollars for which this House has had no opportunity, during the course of considering a bill, to make proposals, to make amendments, to make changes or to call witnesses before a committee. The items are there, and they are subject to a time limit. As I said before this is an exceedingly shabby way to treat the taxpayers of this land.
Finally, the relations between the Auditor General and the government should be altered so that we get better service from this official. A question was asked in the House of Commons yesterday by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Harkness). Today, I am told, there is an article by the Canadian Press containing a statement made by the Auditor General, in which he says the reason he was not able to produce his report at this time is that his staff has been reduced. He says also there is a lack of morale among the staff because of the failure of the government to meet with his request concerning salaries and classifications, as a result of which Public Service Board has not been able to recruit the staff he requires.
I believe this requires a very substantial and serious answer by the government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he would look into it yesterday. It is a very dangerous situation when the Auditor General, the last defence of the taxpayers of our land, is treated in this shabby way. According to the press release the Auditor General's report will not be out until at least May. The Public Accounts Committee is now dealing with the report up to March 31, 1970. Should an election be held this spring or summer, this House will have no opportunity, through the Public Accounts Committee, to deal with
Control of Government Expenditures the report of the Auditor General. It will be left in abeyance until next fall and it will be almost two years after the event before we get around, through our committee, to a study of this report. Since the Auditor General has stated one reason for the delay is the very large number of mistakes in the public accounts, this calls for a very serious examination by this House and some explanation by the government.
Let me close on this note. Today all over the country people have sent, or have prepared, their income tax returns for 1971. They will shortly be coming under the new tax laws which were enacted last session. This is probably neither the time nor the place-and in any event I do not have sufficient time at my disposal-to deal with all the various programs and policies covered by the vast expenditures for the coming fiscal year. However, there is one duty which is obligatory upon every member of this House on both sides. It is to ensure that the taxpayer who is compelled to fork over his money to the government receives a dollar's worth of value for every dollar he pays. This certainly is not the case today. Most people realize there is a responsibility, within the opportunity afforded by their particular earnings, to make a reasonable contribution to limit poverty, distress, unemployment and the problems of the older people. I think the great majority of Canadians are also prepared to attempt to help, at least to some extent, narrow the gap which exists between the various regions of Canada.
Having said that, I think in addition the people of Canada are entitled to, and I demand on their behalf, a fair break. I know there is no government which spends other people's money which is 100 per cent efficient. That is the way it happens. But I think it is a shocking and a shameful thing to see exposed in this House year after year and month after month details of profligacy, of improvidence, of stupidity, of waste, of extravagance and mismanagement and absolutely no corrective measures taken. We demand on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada that this sort of nonsense be brought under control. I have attempted to offer some suggestions. We have criticized the government, and I think we are entitled to do so, but we have not limited ourselves to that. We have offered suggestions as to ways that this situation might be remedied. I suggest that the government should pay some attention to these proposals and give a reasonable answer to the people of Canada before this debate is completed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I look upon the motion made today as a very important one, and I regard it as a motion which we should discuss in terms of looking at our House of Commons operation with respect to the estimates or, to put it in other terms, with respect to the expenditures that parliament is called upon to vote. I realize that in the first part of the motion there is a phrase that seems to get into most opposition motions, namely that we condemn the government, and so we should. No doubt before the day is out some speakers will elaborate on that part of the motion. But I confess that I am more interested in the latter part of the motion, which urges that steps be taken so that we can exercise greater scrutiny and control over
March 7, 1972

Control of Government Expenditures estimates and expenditures. I, therefore, propose to discuss this matter, as I have already said, in terms of looking at the ways in which the House of Commons deals with the estimates.
As hon. members are aware, we made some pretty drastic changes in our procedures a few years ago, and I want to say quite openly that I think in some respects the changes that we made were good. I believe that we did improve the process by which we handle legislation. I think it was a good idea for us to arrange for practically all bills to go to standing committees and for us to eliminate the duplication that we used to have when a bill could be discussed at length in a standing committee and again at length in the committee of the whole House. We got around the complaint that might arise because bills go to standing committees that members not on those committees do not have a chance to speak on the bill by providing for the report stage at which it is possible for any member, by putting down a motion, to achieve a discussion on a phase of the bill in which he is interested. That is not before us today, but I felt that I would like to say that I think we did a good job in the changes we made with respect to the legislative process.
However, I think we have not succeeded to the same extent-in fact I think we have not succeeded at all-in our efforts to find a better way to deal with the estimates or the expenditures which parliament is called upon to vote. I welcome the attendance in the House this afternoon of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), and I hope he will take the remarks I wish to offer in the vein in which I present them. I present them not as an attack upon the government but rather as a plea that the House of Commons as a whole take a new look at the whole question of how we handle our expenditures. I am frequently twitted about the fact that I have been around here for a few years. As I said last night, I am only beginning my stay in parliament, for I hope to be around for several decades yet.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
sleeve was that it could say to the government, "These are the departments we want to deal with on the floor of the House of Commons in this particular session". I think that system worked fairly well. Perhaps modification of it would have been a good idea, but the main difficulty with that system, as I say, was that it was transitional only, and we did not renew it.
Then, we moved from that to the present system under which we send all of the estimates to committees, every last one, including the supplementaries, such as were tabled today. We have abolished the committee of supply. By the way, Mr. Speaker, I was a member of the procedural committee that recommended this, and we thought we were producing a method that was better than the former one. We decided that since all members were doing on supply days was making speeches anyway, we would put in their place 25 opposition days; that we would be honest about it and say 25 days are for opposition members to discuss whatever they wish. In return for that, we would let the estimates go to committees and renounce any right to deal with estimates on the floor of the House.
I think that was a mistake. I do not think we should be faulted for having proposed the idea and for having given it a trial. But it has not worked. The estimates go to committees. Perhaps in the first session of a new parliament the estimates of this department or of that one will get a fairly good going over. But so far as parliament as a whole is concerned, the members not on a particular committee get no chance at those estimates. A day comes, therefore, at the end of the session when a vote has to be taken, and unless those members put down motions, as some of us have done on occasion, all these millions or billions of dollars are voted in a very few minutes, without debate at all.
I think it might almost be better not to do it at all, and merely pass one act which provides that whatever estimates the Treasury Board has brought in are deemed to have been passed when the session ends. But I am sure the President of the Treasury Board does not want that authority. All I am saying is that what we do is so ridiculous that we might as well go the whole way. It is time we had a look at the experience we have had, a look at the four methods, assess them, and ask whether there is not some better way than the one we now follow.
I think the present system is no good. I think the second of the regimes I mentioned just a while ago was likewise no good, that is, when we sent all the estimates to committee of supply but with a time limit of 30 days. I think the system that was in effect when I first came here was the best, but it is not possible to go back to it because there are still only 365 days in the year and there is so much more business to be done. But I think something of the order of the third of the systems I described would be a lot better.
I would like to see us arrange for the estimates to go to committees, and I want to make some suggestions about that, but I would like us to make it part of our rules that the opposition has the right every session to name three or four departments-and it does not have to name them until on in the session-that would also be dealt with on the floor of the House of Commons. Whether that would
Control of Government Expenditures be done by a committee of the whole or a committee of supply does not matter. I would even go so far as to say that this should be without time limit. Lengthen the days if necessary. Have morning sittings then, instead of morning sittings in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. If there is anything to the supposition or myth that parliament controls the public purse, we ought to set it on a basis where we really will be doing this kind of thing.
With regard to the committees that handle estimates, they should be looked at as well. Some of my colleagues may develop some of the points in an amendment that I am going to move, namely, that there should be more services for those committees, more space for them. Don't kick us out of this building and put us over in the Confederation building somewhere. Leave us in this building, but provide a building in which committees can operate as they should. There should also be proper time for the committees to do their job. Now, I am back to an old theme that I often proclaim, namely, that there should be times when parliament does not meet but committees do so that they can do their job.
Then, we have to look in particular at the kind of job committees do on estimates. I go on committees that deal with veterans affairs and with health, welfare and pension matters. These are subjects in which I am interested. But when I do go on these committees, what is my interest? My interest is getting all the money I can for veterans, for pensions, for health services, or what have you.
When my farm colleagues go on the Agriculture Committee they are not interested in saving money. They are interested in getting money and services for the agriculture industry. That is part of our job. None of us is going to renounce it. But in my opinion there is a place for a committee on estimates made up of auditor types, public accounts types, members who will devote themselves to this and will scrutinize the estimates the way the Treasury Board is supposed to scrutinize them before they ever get into the book. I believe that whole programs should be looked at with what we sometimes call a fine-toothed comb, if that isn't a mixed metaphor of some sort. The job our committees do now on estimates is not an auditing job. It is not an inspection or scrutinizing job. It is a job that members do because they are interested in the subject of the committee to which the estimates have been referred.
Another fact of life around here is that in any parliament each department gets a pretty thorough going over about once, and then examination tends to peter out. It is repetition. Maybe it would be good enough in a four-year parliament that every department would have one thorough examination with, shall we say, a special committee on estimates, that could have the authority to call for three or four or five different departments that it would examine, not with an eye to getting more dollars for this or that program, but with an eye to close scrutiny of the estimates. This is the type of thing I am advocating. I think we should go back to a combination of reference of estimates to committees and of dealing with three or four departments on the floor of the House of Commons.
I also think, so far as the committees are concerned, that the standing committees generally should have more

March 7, 1972
Control of Government Expenditures time, and space, and services, and that there should be a special estimates committee which again would have the authority to call each session for three or four of the departments to come before it for the kind of close scrutiny that could be given to them by that type of committee.
Now. Sir, it seems to me that this is the kind of thing we ought to consider. I do not put my ideas out as the final answer, and I would certainly be glad to see them modified or amended. However, I do plead that we not go through another Parliament handling or mishandling or failing to handle estimates as we have these past few years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The process of handling supply the way we do on both interim and final estimates is really a joke. The President of the Treasury Board filed supplementary estimates today, getting them in before the end of March, which means that we do not get the three extra days provided in the rules under certain conditions. The day will come when he will ask for a vote for interim supply for the months of April, May and June. He will get it without any debate on the floor of Parliament because that is the rule. By the end of March, he will have his interim supply for the months of April, May and June and by the end of June, because it is in the book, he will get his vote on the main estimates for the balance of the fiscal year, or until the end of next March. We did this with our eyes wide open because we did not like the old system by which money was being voted on at all. I think we are to be commended for getting rid of that farce, but now we have another one.
As I say, I am trying to present this not as a case of confrontation between government and opposition, but I am asking that we discuss our own operation as a House of Commons. The rules that we have were produced by us. In terms of the legislative process, we made tremendous improvements and we do not need to worry about them within the life of a few more Parliaments. Naturally, members will come along who will want to change them, and that is the way it should be, but in terms of the supply process what we have now is not any good at all.
The President of the Treasury Board may not go as far as the judgment I have made, but I think he will agree that he would like something much better. What he has is very convenient; he knows that once Treasury Board produces the estimates his troubles are over. He gets interim supply before the end of March and the main estimates before the end of June. The worst that could happen is that there might have to be one or two votes on the last night in June on some opposed items, but even that process is hard to pursue. We have put them down for the Prices and Incomes Commission and for the Senate, but there are very few items in the estimates that we can oppose entirely. There are a lot of government programs of which we are critical but we cannot put down a motion of opposition for the entire item. The whole system is for the birds. It does not fit the requirements of a Parliament that is supposed to be giving close examination, is sup-

posed to be scrutinizing the estimates and is supposed to fulfil the role of guardian of the public purse.
I shall welcome further comments made during the course of the day about this matter, but since I see my time is about up I had better present the amendment to which I referred. I should like to offer an amendment to the motion presented by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) which suggests in general terms the kind of thing for which I have been arguing. I, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That the motion be amended by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"by amending the Standing Orders of the House of Commons so that the handling of estimates, instead of being perfunctory and ineffective, will be put on a proper basis, including provision for adequate committee time, space and services, and for consideration of certain of the estimates on the floor of the House of Commons."
Now, Sir, hon. members may have other suggestions and those I have set forth could be modified, but in the main I think what we are proposing is clear. We accept the fact that the legislative process, using committees as it does, is good but we are not satisfied with the process by which estimates are handled. We think it could be improved by strengthening committees, by giving them adequate time, space and services. We think the whole process could also be improved by having an arrangement of the kind I have described, namely, that some of the estimates could be dealt with on the floor of the House of Commons at the instigation of the opposition and also that some of the estimates each year could be dealt with by a special committee set up for that purpose.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the motion that has been moved so that the House can discuss these matters today. We hope the House will look favourably on our amendment and, whatever happens on the vote tonight, we hope that this House will make up its mind that if it is not done before the forthcoming election, in the next Parliament we will have to find a better system for carrying out our function as the guardians of the public purse of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion we are debating today, moved by the official opposition, means that Parliament should be empowered to scrutinize thoroughly federal expenditures.
Indeed the motion is worded as follows, and I quote:
This House condemns the Government for its mismanagement and waste of taxpayers money and urges that Parliament take steps to exercise greater scrutiny and control over estimates and expenditures.
The motion refers to a "waste of taxpayers money" and this is just about what is happening throughout the country. Today, I would like to deal briefly with the local initiative projects approved by the federal government.
Some projects had to be submitted first to the provincial authorities, the Municipal Affairs Department in Quebec and similar departments in other provinces, and
March 7, 1972

the minister or his department accepted the projects presented to the federal government.
Later on we had answers such as this one: This project has been refused. A phone call to the department brought this reply: Certain funds earmarked for these projects have been spent and the total of these amounts exceeds the budget-a budget of $50 million for the whole country. It so happened that many important local initiative projects were refused while others less important were accepted.
For example, the creation of snowmobile trails had been requested and certain municipalities or parishes asked for the improvement of community centers. All they wanted was money to pay the salaries since the materials would be supplied by the parish or municipality. This was rejected.
Substantial amounts of money were spent to create jobs and while these were being created the number of unemployed was going up. The reason given is that the number of people entering the labour market is increasing rapidly; so unemployment goes up and at the same time the government tells us it is creating new jobs.
It may be true that new jobs became available because in February, for example, I saw men cutting branches in three or four feet of snow. Our unemployed were in the snow right up to the belt cutting branches. They had to dig to cut branches. It is obvious that the branches will be growing again this spring and that next winter this will provide other jobs.
However, when I saw those unemployed working in temperatures of 25, 30 or 35 degrees below zero I thought it might be wise for the government to undertake, next winter, another local initiatives program to allow these people to work in a heated place, for example, by buying balls of wool and knitting needles and having them knit mittens. There are not anough mittens in politics. We need more.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we probably need a new minister, a minister of balls of wool to ensure fair distribution to those who want to knit. They could knit in a heated place. This would be as intelligent as having them cut branches in the middle of winter.
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has not yet thought of it. In the coming election campaign we will see if he does not promise us a department of balls of wool and knitting needles to take care of the jobless next winter.

speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question? Would he make a suggestion to the government?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
No, but I am ready to suggest the replacement of our present crazy system. My suggestion would be as crazy, but not more.
Mr. Speaker, important projects have been rejected while, I repeat, others which were unimportant were accepted. Who made the decisions?
Some municipalities, for instance, are told: Your project has a fair chance of being accepted. A building project of sorts is then submitted to the Minister of Municipal
Control of Government Expenditures Affairs providing that the government would pay the salaries involved. The municipality concerned is given to understand that the federal government will accept the project. The provincial government gives the go ahead and subsequently an architect is hired. The plans are drawn at a cost of $10,000 to $12,000 which the municipality is called upon to disburse. The plan is then submitted to the provincial government and the minister declares that it is accepted and that it should be immediately forwarded to Ottawa. Two or three weeks elapse-these things take time-after which Ottawa decides to reject the project. The municipality is then compelled to pay $12,000 to an architect for a project that has been rejected. The government does not contribute a cent. That is, once again, a brilliant system: Parishes and municipalities are compelled to run into debts and pay the salaries of architects whom they are obliged, by provincial laws, to hire. This is done with a promise that the project will be accepted, but then it is rejected.
Only recently, I was talking to officials of the department responsible for the Local Initiatives Program, and they admitted to having gone over the budget. They have spent $15 million already, and the minister says he is not going to add a penny.
Mr. Speaker, since we have established a Local Initiatives Program, let us at least respect the projects which make sense. Let us not make petty excuses and say that all the money has been spent. Let us create a budget!
Yesterday we were presented with a $219 million budget designed to make up for the deficits of the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. Strangely enough, we will manage to find the money! Why cannot we do the same thing for serious local initiatives projects-not, of course, for revolutionaries and rebels!
There is a local initiatives project in Mont-Laurier, for instance, where the FLQ leader Pierre Vallieres, who has now been released from jail, has been hired, even though he said: I will never stop working towards the separation of Quebec.
That same night, the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) stated humbly in a television broadcast in Montreal that Pierre Vallieres had a right to work. I do not question this right, but let him go and work for Rene Levesque-not for the federal government.
Vallieres is paid with the Canadian people's money for working towards the destruction of Canada, towards getting Quebec out of the Canadian Confederation. Where do they send him? To the poor people in Mont-Laurier, so that he can see whether it is true that there are poor people there, and why and how they are poor, and so he can give them advice: You know, fellows, the reason you are poor is because of Ottawa. If you were on Rene Levesque's side in order to make the separation of Quebec come about sooner, you would be a little poorer but it would not show so much. This way he tries to stir up people against the country. Ottawa does not raise any objections. They say: It is a Mr. De Serres who is responsible for the project-another notorious separatist, another man who is openly anti-Canadian. And this project gets $46,000 or $48,000 from the federal government.

March 7, 1972
Control of Government Expenditures
The same goes on in my area of Rouyn-Noranda. Small groups of separatists receive federal subsidies for local initiatives projects. They use that money to try to destroy Canada. You meet them in groups of ten, twelve, and they tell you: Ottawa is stupid enough to pay us, but we are not so stupid as to turn it down. And so they accept subsidies from Ottawa to work towards the destruction of Canada. The government has money to finance those projects but when it comes to the parochial complex of Nedelec, in Temiscamingue, it does not. They refuse a subsidy of $52,000, while in a neighbouring parish, they subsidize a skidoo trail, part of which is built on a river! When the ice melts, the trail will disappear. Still, $46,500 were granted for that project.
I have nothing against skidoo trails; I like the sport myself and do some skidooing. But, Mr. Speaker, projects of greater importance than skidoo trails have been truned down. If they were not, all would be well. Skidoo trails are fine indeed for week-end fun, but they are of secondary importance. In a logical system, that is the way things would be. But under our present system, skidoo trails have the priority over parish halls, and municipal or provincial improvements.
Money could be spent towards achieving better understanding between the various elements of Canada, so that all might work towards buttressing Canadian unity. But no, money is spent on projects that are worth very little.
So, Mr. Speaker, I distinctly blame the government for this situation. The opposition is quite right in saying it has been a stupid waste of taxpayers' money. That is what we are protesting against.
Now, let us turn to the area of unemployment insurance. To a question I put this afternoon, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) replied that there were 200 major offices throughout Canada. They have been centralized in the province of Quebec. For our region and the Hull region, the regional office is in Montreal. Anyone applying to the local Rouyn-Noranda office is referred to Montreal. Some people have received no benefits since October 25, a period of four months. We are entering the fifth month, with still no cheques forthcoming.
Yesterday, for instance, an applicant from Larder Lake, a village in the riding of my friend, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), told me that he has been in touch with the Timmins office since October 25. The day before yesterday, he was notified that his case was still pending. They have been processing the case of this applicant for four months. He was advised to apply to a welfare office for assistance pending settlement of his case. Anyone applying to the provincial welfare office is told: "Your unemployment insurance benefits will be coming through." Yes, but when? In the meantime the applicant is required to undertake in writing to make his cheques over to the office when he receives them and he will thus obtain a small cash advance in the meantime. That is the game they are playing with the unemployed.
There is a still more serious case in my region, Quemont Mines which closed down, laying off 350 miners. These people, according to their working contract, had accumulated a fund of $750 each, which they received when they were laid off. They applied to the Manpower

Centre, but they were told: Gentlemen, when you have spent your $750, we will pay you unemployment insurance benefits. Now, the miner who has not found a job the day after his dismissal does not receive any unemployment insurance benefit. On the other hand, the one who has found one continues to receive an income. He is not told that he will not have to pay unemployment insurance as long as his $750 are not spent. Unemployment insurance contributions are required from his first working day. After having paid unemployment insurance contributions during 20 years, those people are denied benefits, not because they are unemployed, but because they have accumulated $750 during that period. That amount is considered as an extension of their wages.
I suggest that the Department of Labour is stealing from the workers of the Quemont and Noranda mines whose wages amounted to $3,000 or $3,500 at the time of their dismissal. This means that the Department of Labour is a department of thieves whose victims are the miners who have spent their lives toiling at 5,000 or 10,000 feet underground, have lost their job and are now receiving $750 for 20 years of work. And then they are told: Gentlemen, you must spend your $750 before you can get unemployment insurance benefits.
I brought this problem to the attention of the minister who told me: Officials have made a decision. What is the use of a minister who cannot make decisions? It is the officials who are going to decide in the case of the Quemont miners! These men have paid their unemployment insurance contributions, which means that it would come to the same if the government or the public servants said: Gentlemen, over your 25 years of work, you have saved $4,000 or $5,000; so we will have to check. Spend your $5,000 and then, we will pay you unemployment insurance benefits.

And, when the time comes for benefits to be paid to them, they are told: Spend your $750 allowance, and then we will start paying you unemployment insurance benefits. The Quemont miners began receiving benefits at the beginning of March when they had lost their jobs in August, in September or in October last year. And this is supposed to be normal!

For political patronage, money is available. To serve man, there is not. Appeals are made to the department, to the minister, to the deputy minister to solve some cases, because one cannot do so by oneself. And, suddenly, one finds that shameful waste is the rule in many fields, in several sectors of the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, no wonder provinces and municipalities are opposing Ottawa. Millions, billions of dollars are thrown away. When we ask the government to spend money for the people instead of taxing them and spending

money for the benefit of a few privileged persons, we are laughed at.
Ten years ago when I was advocating on television that the Canadian economy be given a push, I suggested distributing $100 to each Canadian only once so as to see the results five or six months later. A family of 10 would have received $1,000 of Canadian credit. One of five would have been given $500. We could then have found out if it was a failure or a profitable undertaking. The Liberals laughed at us. Fools!
According to the estimates for the current year, interest on the national debt is $2,335 million. Do we know what that means? $106.43 per person in Canada. It means that a family of 10 must pay $1,064 in interest on the national debt. Do you see any government members rise up to protest against the interest on the national debt? Of course not. If the amount of $106 is paid to financiers, that is fine, but, if it is paid to Canadians, they cannot see it. They are such fat-heads.
Mr. Speaker, government expenditures are tremendous. Out of a budget of $18 billion this year, nearly $2.3 billion will go to pay the interest on the national debt alone. Nobody protests against that. It is the worst waste in the whole budget, in the whole federal administration.
Mr. Speaker, the Creditistes object to this waste and urge, as it is said in the motion, a fair and honest scrutiny of the Canadian government expenditures, in order to serve the whole population.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion we are considering appears to have two aspects. In one of them, the government is roundly condemned for what is described as mismanagement and waste of taxpayers' money. In the other, parliament is urged to take steps to exercise greater scrutiny and control.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) cited instances of expenditures which have been fairly well examined, I think. In every instance they have been explained, and in many instances the course of action taken has been justified. To describe these now, at this late date, as examples of waste, extravagance, inefficiency and the other attributes he was able to find in his dictionary, is not likely to take us very far in this discussion; I do not think it would be helpful if I were to attempt to rehash all this old history again.
Let me put on record some information with regard to government expenditures as a whole. It is true that government expenditures have been rising from year to year, though I suggest they are not rising at so great a rate as the increase in the responsibilities of the government would indicate. This increase in responsibilities results from the growth in population and from economic growth as reflected in the increase in our gross national product. Public expenditures in Canada have been rising quite rapidly in the past few years. However, they have been rising much more slowly in the federal field than has been the case either in the provincial area or in the combined municipal and provincial area.
The average rate of growth of federal expenditures during the period from 1967 to 1971 inclusive was 11.8 per
Control of Government Expenditures cent per year. Of the total federal expenditure, very substantial sums are transferred annually to the provinces and it is the provinces which in the final analysis make these expenditures and control not only their size but their scope and administration. If one subtracts from the total of the federal expenditures I have mentioned transfers to the provinces, one finds that net growth in federal expenditure exclusive of these transfers to the provinces in the year 1967-68 was 7.8 per cent; in the year 1968-69, 11.6 per cent; in the year 1969-70, 9.8 per cent; and in the year 1970-71, 7.8 per cent, for an average net federal expenditure growth rate of 9.3 per cent per annum. That is pretty much the same as the growth rate in our gross national product.
In a similar way, growth of public expenditures by the provinces is rather more spectacular. From an average annual growth rate of 18 per cent per annum, one subtracts the substantial transfers made by provinces to hospitals and local governments for administrative control and expenditure purposes. This leaves a net figure for provincial administration growth rate in the year 1967-68 of 16.9 per cent; in the year 1968-69, 12.9 per cent; in the year 1969-70, 23.5 per cent; and in the year 1970-71, 24.7 per cent, for an average annual growth rate in provincial government public expenditure, not including sums transferred for local control and administrative purposes to hospitals and municipalities, of 19.5 per cent. So, one can see that the expenditures of the federal government, exclusive of transfers to the provinces, have been something in the order of the gross national product growth, but have grown at a conservatively lesser rate than provincial government expenditures.
Another feature I should like to emphasize is that about one-half of our total annual expenditures are derived not from programs put forward in the estimates and under the appropriation acts, but from separate parliamentary statutes that provide for expenditures on a scale, at a rate, and under conditions determined by the particular statute itself. About one-half of our annual expenditures have been devoted to this particular purpose; the other half go toward appropriations under programs contained in the estimates.
Growth in statutory expenditures as against what we might call discretionary expenditures or appropriations in 1967-68 was about 43 per cent of total federal expenditures, rising in 1972-73 to about 482 per cent. So that the amount of discretionary expenditures under the appropriation acts both in relation to public expenditures as between the provinces, municipalities and the federal government, and in relation to the federal government itself as between statutory expenditures under the control of acts of parliament and discretionary expenditures, has been decreasing. Indeed, it has shown the slowest growth of all the expenditures I have described. This is the particular aspect to which the hon. member for Peace River directed his attention.

I would reiterate that I do not believe the case for the motion and the amendment which call for a change in our procedures has been really put forward strongly. I appreciate that the hon. member for Peace River rather was using this as a nominal or adjectival exercise, whereas I had the impression that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) really hoped to improve our system. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O.58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT AND WASTE OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY-NEED FOR MORE PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL OF ESTIMATES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to be involved in the debate of what we believe is a very significant motion.

I feel that, without question, one would be ill advised to come to the conclusion that there has been no waste or mismanagement on a gross scale since there are so many facts and figures which suggest this is a proper conclusion. I was impressed somewhat by the speech given by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). I think one thing stands out. He indicated to us, I believe in all sincerity, that in effect we in this House of Commons are attempting to deal with more than we can accomplish. I think this is a problem which is becoming more severe as we go along, particularly exemplified by the passage of the tax bill which, as I understand it, is an imperfect bill. This is readily admitted. There were amendments upon amendments and there are amendments to come. Yet because of expediency and because of some deadline, we attempted to deal with more than we could accomplish. The end result is imperfect legislation being foisted upon the Canadian public.
I was also very pleased to have the opportunity to listen to my House leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and I was equally impressed with the arguments developed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I have come to the conclusion that if changes are not made in our Parliamentary system we can probably call the exercises which are perpetuated in this House of Commons, facades-facades in the committee, facades in the House of Commons and facades continued by ministers-I say with all due respect-before the television cameras out in the hall. In other words, it would seem that this place is becoming meaningless for the member of parliament. We are here to represent our constituencies, to look at estimates, to project and give constructive criticism, and yet the ideas of a member of parliament are not usually accepted. The direction which he wishes to place before the House and the people of Canada is not accepted, and the implementations he would like to see pursued are not accepted. They come from the Treasury Board.
Without intending to be nasty in any way, I suggest that many members on the government side are frustrated. I do not think I am letting anything out of the bag when I say they want a more meaningful role, and they want an opportunity to debate and question the integrity of the government. They want an opportunity to vote in order to register their concern. However, because of the system which this government perpetuates they are denied this opportunity. It would be easy for me to condemn the government's handling of the Bras d'Or, the Bonaventure and Information Canadian, which are glaring examples of waste and mismanagement. However, I will leave that to other colleagues of mine on this side of the House.
Another very significant statement by the President of the Treasury Board was his acceptance of the fact there has been an increase in the government's responsibilities. He went on and on in respect of several programs, outlining the why's and wherefors. However, he missed mentioning the responsibility that this government has toward our most important asset, that is the human resource. It is in this area that a stinging indictment is due this government because of its shameful and disgraceful attitude towards people. The government should receive the highest condemnation. They should be condemned for their lack of understanding, lack of proper policies in terms of
March 7, 1972

priorities for people who want to work or who have been in the work force but have lost jobs as a result of this government's fiscal and monetary policies. The Government has stood by and watched this happen as a regrettable side effect, and therefore there is deliberation in the creation of the unemployment for 600,000 people.
What disturbs me is that this government, through lack of understanding of its priorities in the spending of money, has deliberately decided not to reward initiative and not to give incentive. As I understand it, the rate of unemployment is unprecedented and, as I pointed out, it will continue to get worse as a result of the lack of understanding of the government of what the priorities should be in terms of the spending of government money. We need an industrial strategy which will take into consideration the tax cuts and incentives, through the co-operation, understanding and assistance of other levels of government, of labour and management, in order to set the first priority of full employment. The words "full employment" are bandied around day by day, and yet there was a stinging indictment in the presentation of the Canadian Labour Congress which, I believe, speaks for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I want to put on the record some of the things they have said in this regard.
